# Counit of Spectrum Adjunction is a Natural Transformation

## 0. Conventions and definitions

Throughout, $\mathbf{Top}$ is the category of topological spaces and continuous maps.

### 0.1 Frames and locales

A **frame** is a complete lattice $A$ (with order $\le$, arbitrary joins $\bigvee$, arbitrary meets $\bigwedge$, bottom $\bot = \bigvee \varnothing$ and top $\top = \bigwedge \varnothing$) in which finite meets distribute over arbitrary joins:
$$a \wedge \bigvee_{i \in I} b_i = \bigvee_{i \in I} (a \wedge b_i) \qquad (a \in A,\ \{b_i\}_{i \in I} \subseteq A).$$

A **frame homomorphism** $h : A \to B$ is a map preserving finite meets and arbitrary joins; explicitly
$$h(\top_A) = \top_B, \qquad h(a \wedge a') = h(a) \wedge h(a'), \qquad h\Big(\bigvee_{i \in I} a_i\Big) = \bigvee_{i \in I} h(a_i)$$
for all $a, a' \in A$ and all families $\{a_i\}_{i \in I} \subseteq A$ (the case $I = \varnothing$ of the last condition gives $h(\bot_A) = \bot_B$). Frame homomorphisms are monotone, since $a \le a'$ iff $a \wedge a' = a$.

Frames and frame homomorphisms form a category $\mathbf{Frm}$, and the category of **locales** is by definition its opposite:
$$\mathbf{Loc} := \mathbf{Frm}^{\mathrm{op}} .$$

Notation. To keep the two directions apart we write objects of $\mathbf{Loc}$ with the same letters as the underlying frames, and for a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $f : A \to B$ we write
$$f^\flat : B \longrightarrow A$$
for the corresponding frame homomorphism. Thus $f \mapsto f^\flat$ is a bijection $\mathbf{Loc}(A,B) \to \mathbf{Frm}(B,A)$, and by the definition of the opposite category
$$(\mathrm{id}_A)^\flat = \mathrm{id}_A, \qquad (g \circ f)^\flat = f^\flat \circ g^\flat \quad \text{for } A \xrightarrow{\;f\;} B \xrightarrow{\;g\;} C \text{ in } \mathbf{Loc}. \tag{0.1}$$
Consequently, two $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphisms are equal if and only if the corresponding frame homomorphisms are equal.

### 0.2 The locale of open sets functor

For a topological space $T = (S, \tau)$, the set $\tau$ of open sets, ordered by inclusion, is a frame: arbitrary joins are unions, finite meets are intersections, $\top = S$, $\bot = \varnothing$, and the frame distributive law is the set-theoretic identity $U \cap \bigcup_i V_i = \bigcup_i (U \cap V_i)$. (Arbitrary meets exist because a poset with all joins has all meets, via $\bigwedge X = \bigvee \{\, y : y \le x \text{ for all } x \in X \,\}$; concretely they are the interiors of the intersections, but we shall not need them. Note that completeness alone is not enough to be a frame — the five-element diamond $M_3$ is a complete lattice in which $a \wedge (b \vee c) \ne (a \wedge b) \vee (a \wedge c)$ — so the distributive law really has to be checked, as just done.) Write $\mathbf{\Omega} T$ for this frame, viewed as an object of $\mathbf{Loc}$.

For a continuous map $f : T \to T'$ of spaces $T = (S,\tau)$, $T' = (S',\tau')$, the preimage map
$$f^{-1} : \tau' \to \tau, \qquad V \mapsto f^{-1}[V]$$
is well defined by continuity and is a frame homomorphism, since preimages commute with arbitrary unions and with intersections and satisfy $f^{-1}[S'] = S$. The **locale of open sets functor** $\mathbf{\Omega} : \mathbf{Top} \to \mathbf{Loc}$ is defined on objects by $T \mapsto \mathbf{\Omega}T$ and on morphisms by letting $\mathbf{\Omega} f : \mathbf{\Omega} T \to \mathbf{\Omega} T'$ be the $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism with
$$(\mathbf{\Omega} f)^\flat = f^{-1} : \mathbf{\Omega}T' \to \mathbf{\Omega}T . \tag{0.2}$$
This is functorial: $(\mathrm{id}_T)^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_\tau$ and $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$, which by $(0.1)$ says exactly $\mathbf{\Omega}(\mathrm{id}_T) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{\Omega}T}$ and $\mathbf{\Omega}(g \circ f) = \mathbf{\Omega}g \circ \mathbf{\Omega}f$.

### 0.3 The spectrum functor

Let $\mathbf{2} = \{0, 1\}$ with $0 < 1$; this is a frame ($\top = 1$, $\bot = 0$, $\bigvee X = 1$ iff $1 \in X$, and $x \wedge y = \min\{x,y\}$; distributivity is immediate).

A **point** of a locale $A$ is a frame homomorphism $p : A \to \mathbf{2}$. Write
$$\mathrm{pt}(A) := \mathbf{Frm}(A, \mathbf{2})$$
for the set of points, and for $a \in A$ put
$$\Sigma^A_a := \{\, p \in \mathrm{pt}(A) : p(a) = 1 \,\} \subseteq \mathrm{pt}(A).$$
We drop the superscript when the locale is clear.

**Lemma 0.1.** $\tau_A := \{\, \Sigma^A_a : a \in A \,\}$ is a topology on $\mathrm{pt}(A)$.

*Proof.* Each $p \in \mathrm{pt}(A)$ satisfies $p(\top) = 1$, so $\Sigma_\top = \mathrm{pt}(A)$; and $p(\bot) = 0$, so $\Sigma_\bot = \varnothing$. For $a, b \in A$,
$$p \in \Sigma_{a \wedge b} \iff p(a) \wedge p(b) = p(a \wedge b) = 1 \iff p(a) = 1 \text{ and } p(b) = 1 \iff p \in \Sigma_a \cap \Sigma_b,$$
using that in $\mathbf 2$ we have $x \wedge y = 1$ iff $x = y = 1$. Hence $\Sigma_{a \wedge b} = \Sigma_a \cap \Sigma_b$, so $\tau_A$ is closed under binary (hence, with $\Sigma_\top$, under all finite) intersections. For a family $\{a_i\}_{i \in I} \subseteq A$,
$$p \in \Sigma_{\bigvee_i a_i} \iff \bigvee_i p(a_i) = p\Big(\bigvee_i a_i\Big) = 1 \iff \exists i \in I : p(a_i) = 1 \iff p \in \bigcup_{i \in I} \Sigma_{a_i},$$
using that a join in $\mathbf 2$ equals $1$ iff one of its members is $1$. Hence $\Sigma_{\bigvee_i a_i} = \bigcup_i \Sigma_{a_i}$, so an arbitrary union of members of $\tau_A$ again lies in $\tau_A$ (and taking $I = \varnothing$ recovers $\varnothing = \Sigma_\bot \in \tau_A$). Thus $\tau_A$ is a topology. $\qquad\blacksquare$

The **spectrum** of the locale $A$ is the space
$$\operatorname{Sp} A := (\mathrm{pt}(A), \tau_A).$$

For a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $f : A \to B$, with associated frame homomorphism $f^\flat : B \to A$, define
$$\operatorname{Sp} f : \mathrm{pt}(A) \to \mathrm{pt}(B), \qquad p \mapsto p \circ f^\flat . \tag{0.3}$$
This is well defined: a composite of frame homomorphisms is a frame homomorphism, so $p \circ f^\flat \in \mathbf{Frm}(B, \mathbf 2) = \mathrm{pt}(B)$.

**Lemma 0.2.** $\operatorname{Sp} f$ is continuous; indeed for every $b \in B$,
$$(\operatorname{Sp} f)^{-1}\big[\Sigma^B_b\big] = \Sigma^A_{f^\flat(b)} . \tag{0.4}$$

*Proof.* For $p \in \mathrm{pt}(A)$,
$$p \in (\operatorname{Sp} f)^{-1}\big[\Sigma^B_b\big] \iff (\operatorname{Sp} f)(p) \in \Sigma^B_b \iff \big(p \circ f^\flat\big)(b) = 1 \iff p\big(f^\flat(b)\big) = 1 \iff p \in \Sigma^A_{f^\flat(b)} .$$
Since every open set of $\operatorname{Sp} B$ is of the form $\Sigma^B_b$ (Lemma 0.1), every such preimage is open in $\operatorname{Sp}A$, i.e. $\operatorname{Sp}f$ is continuous. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 0.3.** $\operatorname{Sp} : \mathbf{Loc} \to \mathbf{Top}$ is a functor.

*Proof.* Objects and morphisms are as above. For $\mathrm{id}_A$ we have $(\mathrm{id}_A)^\flat = \mathrm{id}_A$ by $(0.1)$, so $(\operatorname{Sp} \mathrm{id}_A)(p) = p \circ \mathrm{id}_A = p$, i.e. $\operatorname{Sp} \mathrm{id}_A = \mathrm{id}_{\operatorname{Sp} A}$. For $A \xrightarrow{f} B \xrightarrow{g} C$ in $\mathbf{Loc}$ and $p \in \mathrm{pt}(A)$, using $(0.1)$,
$$\big(\operatorname{Sp}(g \circ f)\big)(p) = p \circ (g \circ f)^\flat = p \circ \big(f^\flat \circ g^\flat\big) = \big(p \circ f^\flat\big) \circ g^\flat = \big(\operatorname{Sp} g\big)\big((\operatorname{Sp} f)(p)\big),$$
so $\operatorname{Sp}(g \circ f) = \operatorname{Sp} g \circ \operatorname{Sp} f$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Consequently $\mathbf{\Omega} \operatorname{Sp} : \mathbf{Loc} \to \mathbf{Loc}$ is a functor, being the composite of the functors $\operatorname{Sp}$ and $\mathbf{\Omega}$.

### 0.4 The counit

For a locale $A$ define a map
$$\sigma_A^\flat : A \to \mathbf{\Omega} \operatorname{Sp} A = \tau_A, \qquad a \mapsto \Sigma^A_a . \tag{0.5}$$
The **counit of the spectrum adjunction** has $A$-component the $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism
$$\sigma_A : \mathbf{\Omega} \operatorname{Sp} A \to A \quad\text{with}\quad (\sigma_A)^\flat = \sigma_A^\flat .$$
(That this is legitimate is Lemma 1.1 below; the notation is consistent with $\S 0.1$.)

## 1. The components are morphisms of $\mathbf{Loc}$

**Lemma 1.1.** For every locale $A$ the map $\sigma^\flat_A : A \to \tau_A$, $a \mapsto \Sigma_a$, is a frame homomorphism. Hence $\sigma_A$ is a well-defined morphism $\mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A \to A$ of $\mathbf{Loc}$.

*Proof.* By Lemma 0.1 the map indeed lands in $\tau_A = \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A$, and the computations in the proof of Lemma 0.1 give precisely
$$\sigma^\flat_A(\top_A) = \Sigma_\top = \mathrm{pt}(A) = \top_{\tau_A}, \qquad \sigma^\flat_A(a \wedge b) = \Sigma_{a \wedge b} = \Sigma_a \cap \Sigma_b = \sigma^\flat_A(a) \wedge \sigma^\flat_A(b),$$
$$\sigma^\flat_A\Big(\bigvee_{i \in I} a_i\Big) = \Sigma_{\bigvee_i a_i} = \bigcup_{i \in I} \Sigma_{a_i} = \bigvee_{i \in I} \sigma^\flat_A(a_i),$$
where we use that in the frame $\tau_A$ the top element is the whole space, finite meets are intersections and arbitrary joins are unions. So $\sigma^\flat_A$ preserves finite meets and arbitrary joins, i.e. it is a frame homomorphism $A \to \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A$; equivalently, by $\S0.1$, it is (the frame homomorphism underlying) a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $\sigma_A : \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A \to A$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

## 2. Naturality

**Theorem.** $\sigma = (\sigma_A)_{A \in \mathbf{Loc}} : \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp} \to \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$ is a natural transformation: for every $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $f : A \to B$ the square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A & \xrightarrow{\ \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}f\ } & \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}B\\
\downarrow{\scriptstyle \sigma_A} & & \downarrow{\scriptstyle \sigma_B}\\
A & \xrightarrow{\qquad f \qquad} & B
\end{array}$$
commutes in $\mathbf{Loc}$, i.e.
$$\sigma_B \circ \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp} f = f \circ \sigma_A. \tag{2.1}$$

*Proof.* By Lemma 1.1 every $\sigma_A$ is a morphism $(\mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp})(A) \to \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(A)$ of $\mathbf{Loc}$, so $\sigma$ is a family of morphisms of the required type; it remains to verify $(2.1)$.

Both sides of $(2.1)$ are $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphisms $\mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A \to B$, so by $\S0.1$ it suffices to prove the equality of the corresponding frame homomorphisms $B \to \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A$. Using $(0.1)$ twice,
$$\big(\sigma_B \circ \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}f\big)^\flat = \big(\mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}f\big)^\flat \circ \sigma_B^\flat, \qquad \big(f \circ \sigma_A\big)^\flat = \sigma_A^\flat \circ f^\flat,$$
so $(2.1)$ is equivalent to
$$\big(\mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}f\big)^\flat \circ \sigma_B^\flat = \sigma_A^\flat \circ f^\flat : B \to \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A. \tag{2.2}$$
By $(0.2)$ applied to the continuous map $\operatorname{Sp}f : \operatorname{Sp}A \to \operatorname{Sp}B$,
$$\big(\mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}f\big)^\flat = \big(\mathbf{\Omega}(\operatorname{Sp}f)\big)^\flat = (\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1} : \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}B \to \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}A .$$
Now let $b \in B$ be arbitrary. Then, by $(0.5)$, $(0.4)$ and $(0.5)$ again,
$$\Big(\big(\mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp}f\big)^\flat \circ \sigma_B^\flat\Big)(b) = (\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\big[\Sigma^B_b\big] \overset{(0.4)}{=} \Sigma^A_{f^\flat(b)} = \sigma^\flat_A\big(f^\flat(b)\big) = \big(\sigma^\flat_A \circ f^\flat\big)(b).$$
Since $b \in B$ was arbitrary, $(2.2)$ holds, hence so does $(2.1)$.

As $f : A \to B$ was an arbitrary morphism of $\mathbf{Loc}$, all naturality squares commute, and therefore $\sigma : \mathbf{\Omega}\operatorname{Sp} \to \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$ is a natural transformation. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### 2.1 Unwinding the key step

For the reader who prefers the verification without the $(\cdot)^\flat$ bookkeeping: the content of $(2.2)$ evaluated at $b \in B$ is the equality of two open subsets of $\operatorname{Sp}A$, and for $p \in \mathrm{pt}(A)$ one has the chain of equivalences
$$p \in (\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\big[\Sigma^B_b\big]
\iff (p \circ f^\flat)(b) = 1
\iff p\big(f^\flat(b)\big) = 1
\iff p \in \Sigma^A_{f^\flat(b)},$$
the first step by the definition $(0.3)$ of $\operatorname{Sp}f$ together with the definition of $\Sigma^B_b$, and the last by the definition of $\Sigma^A_{f^\flat(b)}$. So the two sides of $(2.2)$ have the same elements, hence are equal. Note that no property of $f^\flat$ beyond being a function was used here; the frame-homomorphism properties of $f^\flat$ are needed only to know that $\operatorname{Sp}f$ is a well-defined, continuous map and that $\sigma^\flat_A$, $\sigma^\flat_B$ are frame homomorphisms.

## 3. Remark: other standard descriptions of the points of a locale

The result is insensitive to which of the three usual equivalent definitions of "point of a locale" is used, because the bijections below carry the sets $\Sigma_a$ and the maps $\operatorname{Sp}f$ to each other. Let $A$ be a frame.

1. **Frame homomorphisms $p : A \to \mathbf 2$** (used above).

2. **Completely prime filters.** A subset $F \subseteq A$ is a completely prime filter if $\top \in F$, $\bot \notin F$, $F$ is upward closed, $a, b \in F \Rightarrow a \wedge b \in F$, and $\bigvee_{i \in I} a_i \in F \Rightarrow a_i \in F$ for some $i \in I$. The assignments $p \mapsto p^{-1}[\{1\}]$ and $F \mapsto \chi_F$ (the characteristic function of $F$) are mutually inverse bijections between $\mathbf{Frm}(A,\mathbf 2)$ and the set of completely prime filters of $A$: the five filter conditions are exactly the statements that $\chi_F$ preserves $\top$, $\bot$, is monotone, preserves binary meets, and preserves arbitrary joins (monotonicity being implied by meet-preservation, and preservation of the empty join being the condition $\bot \notin F$). Under this bijection $\Sigma_a$ becomes $\{F : a \in F\}$, and $\operatorname{Sp}f$ becomes $F \mapsto (f^\flat)^{-1}[F]$.

3. **Prime elements.** Call $q \in A$ prime if $q \ne \top$ and $a \wedge b \le q$ implies $a \le q$ or $b \le q$. Given $p \in \mathbf{Frm}(A, \mathbf 2)$ put $q_p := \bigvee p^{-1}[\{0\}]$; then $p(q_p) = \bigvee\{p(a) : p(a) = 0\} = 0$, so $p^{-1}[\{0\}] = \{a \in A : a \le q_p\}$ (one inclusion by definition of $q_p$, the other by monotonicity of $p$), whence $q_p \ne \top$ (as $p(\top) = 1$) and $q_p$ is prime (if $a \wedge b \le q_p$ then $p(a) \wedge p(b) = 0$, so $p(a) = 0$ or $p(b) = 0$). Conversely a prime $q$ yields $p_q$ with $p_q(a) = 0$ iff $a \le q$, which is a frame homomorphism because $\top \not\le q$, because $\bigvee_i a_i \le q$ iff $a_i \le q$ for all $i$, and by primeness for binary meets. These assignments are mutually inverse, and $\Sigma_a$ corresponds to $\{q \text{ prime} : a \not\le q\}$ while $\operatorname{Sp}f$ corresponds to $q \mapsto \bigvee\{b \in B : f^\flat(b) \le q\}$.

In each presentation the verification of the naturality square is literally the computation of $\S 2.1$ transported along these bijections; e.g. in presentation 2 it reads
$$(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\big[\{F' : b \in F'\}\big] = \big\{F : b \in (f^\flat)^{-1}[F]\big\} = \big\{F : f^\flat(b) \in F\big\},$$
which is the open set of $\operatorname{Sp}A$ corresponding to $f^\flat(b) \in A$, as required.

## 4. Remark: relation to the adjunction

Nothing above used the adjunction $\mathbf{\Omega} \dashv \operatorname{Sp}$; naturality of $\sigma$ is an independent statement about the family $(\sigma_A)$, and indeed it is one of the ingredients needed to *establish* that $\sigma$ is the counit of an adjunction (together with naturality of the unit $\eta_T : T \to \operatorname{Sp}\mathbf{\Omega}T$, $x \mapsto (U \mapsto [\![x \in U]\!])$, and the two triangle identities). $\blacksquare$
